spec: Given a list of integers, return True if each element is strictly greater than the next (no equal adjacent values allowed), and False otherwise. An empty list or a single-element list is considered strictly sorted.
Given a list of (a, b) tuples, return True if the second elements b form a non-decreasing sequence across the list in order, and False otherwise. A list with 0 or 1 tuples is considered sorted.

Given two lists of integers that are each already sorted in ascending order, return a single ascending list containing every distinct value that appears in either list, with no duplicates. Either list may be empty.

Given two lists of integers that are each already sorted in descending order, merge them into a single descending list containing all elements from both (duplicates are kept). When elements are equal, an element from the first list comes before an equal element from the second list. Either list may be empty.

Given two lists of integers that are each already sorted in ascending order of absolute value, merge them into a single list ordered by ascending absolute value. When two elements have equal absolute value, an element from the first list comes before one from the second list. Either list may be empty.

Given a list of strings, return them sorted by the number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u, case-insensitive) they contain, ascending. If two strings have the same vowel count, order them alphabetically. The input list may be empty.

Given a list of (x, y) integer coordinate tuples, return them sorted by Manhattan distance from the origin (|x| + |y|), ascending. Break ties by comparing x ascending, then y ascending. The input list may be empty.
Given a dictionary mapping strings to integers, return a list of (key, value) tuples ordered by value descending, breaking ties by key ascending. The input dictionary may be empty.
Given a list of integers, return a sorted list (ascending) of the distinct values present, with no duplicates. The input list may be empty.
Given a non-empty list of integers, return the value that occurs most often. If multiple values are tied for the highest frequency, return the smallest such value.

Given a list of strings, return them sorted case-insensitively (comparing lowercase forms), and if two strings are equal when lowercased, break the tie by comparing them normally (case-sensitively, where uppercase letters sort before lowercase). The input list may be empty.

Given a list of strings, return them sorted according to the alphabetical order of each string reversed (compare the strings as if each were spelled backwards), but return the original (non-reversed) strings in that order. The input list may be empty.

Given a non-empty list of integers and a percentile p between 1 and 100, sort the list ascending and select the value at the position given by the nearest-rank method: the 1-based index equal to the ceiling of p/100 times the number of elements (clamped between 1 and the list length). Return that value.

Given a non-empty list of integers, compute its median (using the odd/even averaging rule), then return the values sorted by their absolute difference from that median, ascending. If two values have the same absolute difference, the smaller value comes first.

Given a list of rows, where each row is a list of integers, return the rows sorted by the sum of their elements, ascending. If two rows have the same sum, order them by their first element ascending (treat an empty row as having first element 0). The input list of rows may be empty.

Given a list of non-empty rows, where each row is a list of integers, return the rows sorted by their first element ascending. If two rows share the same first element, order them by the sum of their elements ascending.

Given a list of integers, return a new list where all negative numbers come first (sorted ascending among themselves), followed by all non-negative numbers (also sorted ascending among themselves). The input list may be empty.
Given a list of strings, return them sorted so that longer strings come first. Among strings of the same length, order them alphabetically ascending. The input list may be empty.

Given a list of strings and a single character ch, return the strings sorted by how many times ch appears in them, descending. If two strings contain the same count of ch, order them alphabetically ascending. The input list of strings may be empty.

Given a non-empty list of integers and a value x, compute the percentage of elements in the list that are strictly smaller than x (count divided by the list length, times 100), rounded to 2 decimal places, and return that percentage.

Given a list of full name strings each formatted as 'First Last' (exactly one space separating the two words), return the list sorted by the last name (surname) ascending, breaking ties by first (given) name ascending. Return the original full name strings in that order.
visible_tests: assert sort_names_by_surname_then_given(['John Smith', 'Jane Adams']) == ['Jane Adams', 'John Smith']
assert sort_names_by_surname_then_given(['Amy Zoo', 'Bob Zoo']) == ['Amy Zoo', 'Bob Zoo']

spec: Given a list of non-negative integers, return them sorted by the product of their decimal digits, ascending (a digit of 0 makes the product 0). If two numbers have the same digit product, order them by value ascending. The input list may be empty.

Given a list of (a, b) integer tuples, return them sorted by the first element descending. If two tuples have the same first element, order them by the second element ascending. The input list may be empty.

Given a list of integers and a non-negative integer k (at most the length of the list), sort the list ascending, then split it into the k largest values (returned in descending order) and the remaining smaller values (returned in ascending order). Return a tuple (top_k_descending, rest_ascending).

Given a list of (time, priority, name) event tuples, return the names ordered by time ascending. If two events share the same time, order by priority ascending (a lower priority number means it is handled first). If both tie, order by name ascending. The input list may be empty.

Given a list of strings each representing an integer (optionally with a leading minus sign), return them sorted by their integer value ascending. If two strings represent the same integer value, order them by their original string form ascending. The input list may be empty.

Given a list of integers and a positive integer k, return the list sorted by the remainder of each value modulo k, ascending. If two values have the same remainder, order them by their actual value ascending. The input list may be empty.

Given a list of (name, score) tuples with unique names, return a dictionary mapping each name to its dense rank based on score descending (the highest score gets rank 1, and ties share the same rank with no gap before the next distinct score). The input list may be empty.

Given a list of (start, end) integer interval tuples, return True if the list is sorted by start ascending and no two consecutive intervals overlap (an interval may touch the next one, ending exactly where the next begins, but not extend past its start). Return False otherwise. A list with 0 or 1 intervals is considered valid.

Given a list of (name, price, stock) tuples, return the names ordered by price ascending. If two items share the same price, order by stock descending. If price and stock both tie, order alphabetically by name. The input list may be empty.

Given a list of integers, return True if the list is a rotation of some non-decreasing sorted sequence (that is, it can be split into two consecutive parts, possibly empty, that when swapped give a non-decreasing list), and False otherwise. A list of length 0 or 1 is always considered such a rotation.

Given a list of integers, return the list of distinct values ordered so that the value occurring most often in the input comes first. If two distinct values occur the same number of times, the one that appeared earlier (by index of first occurrence) in the input comes first. The input list may be empty.

Given a list of strings and a positive integer n (at most the number of distinct strings), return the n most frequent strings ordered from most frequent to least frequent. If two strings occur the same number of times, order them alphabetically ascending.
Given a list of integers, return them sorted by absolute value descending. If two values have the same absolute value, the smaller (more negative) one comes first. The input list may be empty.

Given a list of (flag, value) tuples where flag is a boolean, return a list of values where all entries with flag True come first (sorted ascending among themselves), followed by all entries with flag False (also sorted ascending among themselves). The input list may be empty.

Given two lists of integers that are each already sorted in ascending order, and a positive integer k (at most the combined length of both lists), return the k-th smallest value (1-indexed) among all elements from both lists combined.
Given a list of strings, return them sorted so that shorter strings come first. Among strings of the same length, order them in reverse alphabetical order (descending). The input list may be empty.
Given a list of (title, year) tuples, return them sorted by year ascending. If two entries share the same year, order them alphabetically by title. The input list may be empty.

Given a list of (category, value) tuples where category is a string and value is an integer, group the values by category, sort each category's values ascending, and return a dictionary mapping each category to its sorted list of values. The input list may be empty.

Given a list of integers and a target integer, return the list sorted by absolute difference from the target ascending. If two values are equally close to the target, the smaller value comes first. The input list may be empty.
